extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural students, historians, and educated travellers interested in Venetian/Gothic architecture and restoration
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for identifying, dating, and assessing Venetian Gothic windows, their orders, materials, mouldings, structural behaviour, and decorative treatment; intended for study, conservation, or revival design. Emphasises formal features (orders, cusps, tracery), material use (brick, stone, marble), and constructive/esthetic judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slope of window flanks as primary Gothic indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: “it will be observed that they differ not merely in mouldings, but in slope of sides, and this latter difference is by far the most material. For in the example 3 h there is hardly any true Gothic expression; it is still the pure Byzantine arch, with a point thrust up through it: but the moment the flanks slope, as in 3 d, the Gothic expression is definite...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use slope of the sides (flanks) as a key diagnostic: slight slope → nascent Gothic; pronounced slope → definite Gothic. Distinguish forms that only have a pointed apex from those where the flanks slope inward — the latter signal a shift in the architectural school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order classification of windows (third, fourth, fifth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Windows are classifiable into orders (third, fourth, fifth, etc.), each with characteristic forms, mouldings, and proportions; the fifth order is the nearest approximation to a perfect Gothic form in Venice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the order by comparing arch-line, cusp form, tracery, and relationship to neighbouring forms; orders can combine (e.g., fifth order as combination of third and fourth). Use plates/figures as typological references to assign order and relative dating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mouldings vs structural slope — both important but slope most material
rubrics_metrics.description: Windows differ not merely in mouldings, but in slope of sides, and this latter difference is by far the most material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While decorative mouldings matter for stylistic nuance, prioritise geometric/profile features (side slope) when assessing Gothic character and lineage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive development of forms as dating criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: “This slope of the flanks occurs, first, in so slight a degree as to be hardly perceptible, and gradually increases until, reaching the form 3 e at the close of the thirteenth century, the window is perfectly prepared for a transition into the fifth order.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate degree of morphological change (e.g., slope, cusp thinning, tracery perforation) to place a window within a developmental sequence and estimate relative age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cusp solidity as age test
rubrics_metrics.description: “Generally speaking, the condition in which the cusp is found is a useful test of age, when compared with other points; the more solid it is, the more ancient: but the massive form is often found associated with the perforated, as late as the beginning of the fourteenth century.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use solidity/thickness of cusps (solid → older; perforated/thin → later and often decorative) alongside other features for dating; beware of overlapping conditions where both solid and perforated forms coexist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and expressive potential of brick
rubrics_metrics.description: “The real use of brick... in the ancient architecture of the clay districts of Italy, every possible adaptation of the material is found exemplified... moulded bricks, wrought into flower-work and tracery as fine as raised patterns upon china.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value brick as a legitimate expressive medium: moulded bricks can form delicate tracery and ornament; judicious use of brick (including cast or hand-moulded units) is a sign of refined workmanship rather than inferiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material differentiation: stone shafts and pilasters vs brick arches
rubrics_metrics.description: “These windows ... are entirely wrought in brick, with exquisite mouldings, not cast, but moulded in the clay by the hand, so that there is not one piece of the arch like another; the pilasters and shafts being, as usual, of stone.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess combination of materials: brick for arch and moulding work, stone for shafts/pilasters/bases. This combination is characteristic and often original — do not assume brick means low quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and detachment of shafts from glazing
rubrics_metrics.description: “I have drawn it from the side, in order that the great depth of the arches may be seen, and the clear detaching of the shafts from the sheets of glass behind. The latter, as well as the balcony, are comparatively modern; but there is no doubt that if glass were used in the old window, it was set behind the shafts, at the same depth.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reconstructing or assessing windows, note that original glazing (if present) sat behind the shafts; arches are deep and shafts stand proud of the glazing plane — preserve/reinstate this spatial relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracery/perforation evolution and decorative role
rubrics_metrics.description: “the penetration of the cusp, leaving only a silver thread of stone traced on the darkness of the window... the cusp ceases to have any constructive use, and is merely decorative... the steps of transition... are noticed... the thinning of the stone, which is not cut through until it is thoroughly emaciated.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise progression from structural cusps to slender decorative tracery; use presence/degree of perforation as stylistic/dating evidence and to inform sensitive restoration (retain decorative thin traceries where original).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enrichment of spandrils and inter-arch intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: “how the intervals between the arches, now left blank by the abandonment of the Byzantine sculptures, should be enriched... examples: spandrils filled by the emblems of the four Evangelists in deep relief; other with an intricate tracery of involved quatrefoils.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider several historically-grounded strategies for treating inter-arch panels: figurative reliefs, intricate quatrefoil tracery, or adopting the Ducal Palace arcade model (which became the established model). Match enrichment method to date, building importance, and regional typology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopted model from Ducal Palace as standard for important works
rubrics_metrics.description: “the builder of the Ducal Palace... designed the great arcade... which thenceforward became the established model for every work of importance in Venice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For work of claimed importance or civic prominence, use the Ducal Palace arcade arrangement/tracery as the canonical reference for proportion, tracery pattern, and interval enrichment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand‑moulded brickwork as sign of craftsmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: “mouldings, not cast, but moulded in the clay by the hand, so that there is not one piece of the arch like another...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise irregular, non‑identical units as evidence of skilled hand-work; resist replacement with perfectly identical cast units when authenticity is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balconies between shafts as characteristic element
rubrics_metrics.description: “The smaller balconies between the great shafts in the lower example in Plate XVIII. are original and characteristic...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where authentic, retain small balconies set between large shafts as a characteristic compositional device of Venetian Gothic façades; reinstatement should follow original positioning and scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform family resemblance across sizes and functions
rubrics_metrics.description: “Under every condition of importance, through every variation of size, the forms and mode of decoration of all the features were universally alike; not servilely alike, but fraternal... No fragment of the period is preserved, in which the windows... have not the noble cusped arch of the fifth order.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor designs that maintain a coherent family resemblance (proportions, cusped arch language, ornament vocabulary) across building scales and functions rather than eclectic mixes; consistency is a historic hallmark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color and material contrast as compositional effect
rubrics_metrics.description: “Its effect is dependent entirely on color. Disks of green serpentine are inlaid on the field of purple alabaster; and the pillars are alternately of red marble with white capitals, and of white marble with red capitals.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrasting stones and inlays (colored marbles, serpentine, alabaster disks) to achieve visual richness where sculpture is minimal; color/material patterning is historically appropriate for Venetian palaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pointed arch superiority for strength and durability
rubrics_metrics.description: “let him be assured... if he find there is more to be enjoyed in the Gothic window, there is also more to be trusted. It is the best and strongest building... the general strength of the pointed arch as opposed to that of the level lintel of the square window... the common square window is the worst; and its level head of brickwork... is the weakest way of covering a space.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer pointed arches over level lintels for durability and structural reliability, especially when building with imperfect materials. Treat square-headed openings with caution in terms of long-term stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pointed arch compatible with modern glazing
rubrics_metrics.description: “Neither can the objection... that it will not admit the convenient adjustment of modern sashes and glass, hold for an instant.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not consider pointed arches incompatible with modern sash/glazing systems; adapt sash/double glazing to fit within or behind the arch geometry while preserving visual and structural characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in materials and economy: moral/technical requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: “dishonesty and false economy will no more build safely in Gothic than in any other style... buildings, raised as I would have them, would stand unshaken for a thousand years; and the buildings raised by the architects who oppose them will not stand for one hundred and fifty...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insist on honest use of materials and proper construction practice; avoid cheap expedients (stucco, bad iron work, rotten timbers) that undermine longevity irrespective of chosen style. Sound construction is a prerequisite for formal success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural centralization pattern for window composition
rubrics_metrics.description: “observe the curious following out, even in this minor instance, of the great law of centralization... There is a central shaft, a pilaster on each side, and then the wall.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose window groups with a central organizing element (central shaft) flanked by pilasters, then plain wall — this centralized ordering is a recurring structural/compositional rule in Venetian palaces and should guide analysis and restoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of local mainland types as source models
rubrics_metrics.description: “of these, fig. 4 is taken from the outer arcade of San Fermo of Verona, to show the condition of mainland architecture, from which all these Venetian types were borrowed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tracing influences or selecting appropriate precedents for design/restoration, look to mainland Italian (Veronese) prototypes for forms and details that were adapted into Venetian Gothic — cross-reference regional schools.
